incidents.title: Server 1 is overloaded
incidents.brief: Three app servers are live, but 90% of traffic still routes to Server 1.
incidents.constraint: The other servers are almost idle.
incidents.question: What is the root cause?

choices.label: Put an L7 load balancer using least-connections in front
choices.resultBody: The Layer 7 load balancer distributes incoming requests evenly across the server fleet, stabilizing CPU utilization across all nodes.

choices.label: Add a Redis cache in front of Server 1's hottest queries
choices.resultBody: Cached queries shave some latency, but routing still sends 90% of traffic to Server 1, which stays pegged while Servers 2 and 3 sit idle.

choices.label: Publish all three server IPs as round-robin DNS A records
choices.resultBody: Client DNS caching (ISPs and browsers) binds thousands of users to a single IP address for hours, preserving the traffic imbalance.

hints: Traffic is not shared evenly.
Healthy copies sit idle.
Put a balancer in front.

incidents.title: One server dies
incidents.brief: An instance fails in the middle of a traffic burst and requests start failing immediately.
incidents.constraint: The remaining servers are healthy but not all traffic is rerouted.
incidents.question: How do you route around the failure?

choices.label: Active health checks that evict a dead node within 3 s
choices.resultBody: The load balancer detects failed HTTP health checks and immediately routes traffic away from the dead node to healthy surviving instances.

choices.label: Update the DNS A records in Route 53 when a node crashes
choices.resultBody: Manual DNS updates take minutes to execute, and downstream DNS resolver TTL caching keeps sending traffic to the crashed server for up to an hour.

choices.label: Let clients retry failed calls until they reach a live node
choices.resultBody: Without automated server-side failover, 1 in every 3 requests continues hitting the dead node, generating waves of 502 Bad Gateway errors.

hints: Traffic is not shared evenly.
Healthy copies sit idle.
Put a balancer in front.

incidents.title: Mobile clients bypass the public endpoint
incidents.brief: The app has two servers, but mobile traffic is still pointed at the old host directly.
incidents.constraint: The app layer is horizontally scaled but not reachable through the load balancer.
incidents.question: What completes the fix?

choices.label: Point the mobile API hostname at the balancer's VIP
choices.resultBody: Mobile clients now resolve one resilient virtual IP on the balancer, so both servers take traffic and the client no longer depends on server topology.

choices.label: Ship both server IPs hardcoded in the mobile app binary
choices.resultBody: Hardcoding server IP addresses inside mobile apps requires an app store update whenever infrastructure changes, creating permanent failure paths for older app versions.

choices.label: Rotate between server IPs with client-side round-robin
choices.resultTitle: Unsynchronized Balancing & DDoS on Single Node
choices.resultBody: Client-side rotation lacks centralized visibility into backend server health, easily sending traffic storms into degraded nodes.

hints: Traffic is not shared evenly.
Healthy copies sit idle.
Put a balancer in front.

incidents.title: Uneven traffic after a deployment
incidents.brief: A new version is deployed to two servers, but one receives 68% of the traffic.
incidents.constraint: The balancing policy is not consistent and one node gets more than its share.
incidents.question: What is the immediate design problem?

choices.label: Switch round-robin to least-requests with slow-start
choices.resultBody: Least-Requests routing dynamically accounts for request processing duration, sending new requests only to servers with available capacity.

choices.label: Add a per-pod response cache to cut hot-pod work
choices.resultBody: Caching trims per-request work, but the router still sends 68% of requests to one pod, so it stays the first to saturate.

choices.label: Pin each client IP to a pod with source-IP hashing
choices.resultBody: Hashing on source IP pins whole office NATs and mobile carriers to one pod, so the split gets lumpier instead of flatter.

hints: Traffic is not shared evenly.
Healthy copies sit idle.
Put a balancer in front.

incidents.title: Latency climbs after an app restart
incidents.brief: One app server is restarted and the traffic is still mostly directed to the old instance.
incidents.constraint: Healthy nodes are available but get little traffic.
incidents.question: What keeps the system unhealthy?

choices.label: Weighted slow-start that ramps a restarted node over 60 s
choices.resultBody: Slow-Start gently increases traffic weighting over 60 seconds, allowing JIT compilation and database pools to initialize without crashing.

choices.label: Raise the balancer's connection timeout to absorb cold starts
choices.resultBody: Longer timeouts let cold-start requests finish instead of failing, but the restarted node still takes a full share at once and p99 stays high while it warms.

choices.label: Double the restarted pod's CPU limit during its first minute
choices.resultBody: Extra CPU speeds up JIT compilation a little, but the pod still takes its full share of traffic cold and its connection pools start empty.

hints: Traffic is not shared evenly.
Healthy copies sit idle.
Put a balancer in front.

incidents.title: All traffic hits one edge instance
incidents.brief: A single edge service is the main public door, but the remaining edges are not in rotation.
incidents.constraint: The app is scaled yet not balanced.
incidents.question: What is the best fix?

choices.label: Consistent hashing with virtual nodes across all edge proxies
choices.resultBody: Virtual nodes on the hash ring distribute client connections uniformly across the edge fleet, eliminating traffic hot-spotting.

choices.label: Add a hot-standby edge instance that takes over on failure
choices.resultBody: The standby only takes traffic when the primary dies, so one edge still carries every connection and stays saturated.

choices.label: Front the edge with a CDN for dynamic websocket traffic
choices.resultBody: CDNs cannot cache dynamic bi-directional WebSocket connections, so all socket traffic still funnels to the single un-balanced origin node.

hints: Traffic is not shared evenly.
Healthy copies sit idle.
Put a balancer in front.

incidents.title: A region fails but no traffic shift happens
incidents.brief: A regional app server crashes, yet clients continue hitting the bad endpoint for a long time.
incidents.constraint: There is a health check gap.
incidents.question: Which property should the distribution layer provide?

choices.label: Global server load balancing with health-probed GeoDNS
choices.resultBody: GSLB probes detect regional datacenter impairment and dynamically update DNS routing to send global traffic to healthy secondary regions.

choices.label: Retry failed requests from clients with exponential backoff
choices.resultBody: If an entire region's power or network link fails, clients in that geography cannot connect at all, making retries futile without DNS traffic shifting.

choices.label: Fail over to a hardcoded backup IP in the second region
choices.resultBody: Failing over to a static IP without health verification risks dumping all global traffic into an unprovisioned or equally degraded secondary region.

hints: Traffic is not shared evenly.
Healthy copies sit idle.
Put a balancer in front.

incidents.title: Traffic spins between two servers
incidents.brief: A two-node system alternates latency spikes even though the nodes are healthy.
incidents.constraint: The routing algorithm is not aware of node health and session stickiness is weak.
incidents.question: What should be improved?

choices.label: Cookie session affinity with a consistent-hash fallback
choices.resultBody: Cookie-based session affinity ensures stateful shopping carts and auth sessions remain anchored to the correct backend node.

choices.label: Switch the balancer to least-connections routing
choices.resultBody: Least-connections evens out load, but it still ignores which server holds each session, so users keep bouncing between the two servers' memories.

choices.label: Raise the DNS TTL to 24 hours to freeze client routing
choices.resultBody: High DNS TTLs freeze client routing at ISP levels, preventing rapid failover during incidents while failing to solve multi-server load skew.

hints: Traffic is not shared evenly.
Healthy copies sit idle.
Put a balancer in front.

incidents.title: Cascading failures after one crash
incidents.brief: During a moderate surge, one node dies and the rest absorb too much traffic until they also fail.
incidents.constraint: The load balancer had no failover policy for partial failure.
incidents.question: What design decision prevents this pattern?

choices.label: Load shedding and circuit breakers at the balancer
choices.resultBody: Load shedding returns immediate 429/503 responses to excess traffic, protecting surviving servers from being overwhelmed when one node dies.

choices.label: Vertically scale each survivor to twice the vCPUs
choices.resultBody: Each resize needs a reboot, so every node you upsize leaves the pool mid-surge. The survivors take even more load and the cascade speeds up.

choices.label: Raise balancer connection timeouts so slow calls can finish
choices.resultBody: Holding dead connections open exhausts connection pools and thread workers across all surviving servers, accelerating cascading collapse.

hints: Traffic is not shared evenly.
Healthy copies sit idle.
Put a balancer in front.

incidents.title: Traffic is uneven by geography
incidents.brief: Users in Europe are routed to one node while Asia goes to another, and one node is overloaded.
incidents.constraint: The balancing layer is not aware of region or health.
incidents.question: What is the correct balancing principle?

choices.label: Latency-based GeoDNS to health-checked regional PoPs
choices.resultBody: GeoDNS routes users to the geographically closest datacenter with sub-20ms latency, balancing load evenly across global points of presence.

choices.label: Round-robin all users globally across every region's nodes
choices.resultBody: Naive round-robin routes users to random continents, incurring massive speed-of-light fiber latency penalties.

choices.label: Let users pick a region with a cookie on first visit
choices.resultBody: Manual region selection causes about 25% drop-off at onboarding and never redirects users when their chosen region has an outage.

hints: Traffic is not shared evenly.
Healthy copies sit idle.
Put a balancer in front.

incidents.title: gRPC clients pin to two of eight pods
incidents.brief: RideNow's pricing service takes 24,000 gRPC calls/s through a Kubernetes ClusterIP. HTTP/2 connections live for hours, so after a scale-up 2 of 8 pods sit at 94% CPU while 6 idle near 10%.
incidents.constraint: The calling services can't be redeployed this week; only infrastructure changes are allowed.
incidents.question: Where should the balancing decision happen so the idle pods get work?

choices.label: Per-request L7 balancing through an Envoy gRPC proxy

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Even load per call for an extra proxy hop.

choices.resultTitle: Streams spread across all eight pods
choices.resultBody: Envoy terminates the HTTP/2 connections and sends each gRPC stream to the least-loaded pod, so all 8 pods settle near 38% CPU and deadline errors fall to 0.1%. Cost: one extra proxy hop of about 0.5 ms and another component to run.

choices.label: Add four more pricing pods to the Deployment
choices.resultBody: The four new pods pass readiness, but the existing HTTP/2 connections never reconnect, so they receive almost no calls. Pods 1-2 stay at 93% CPU and deadline errors hold near 6%.

choices.label: Switch kube-proxy to IPVS least-connection balancing
choices.resultBody: IPVS now spreads TCP connections evenly, but one connection from the busiest caller still multiplexes 60% of all calls. Whichever pod holds it stays above 90% CPU because the scheduler never sees individual streams.

hints: The idle pods are healthy and reachable.
kube-proxy picks a pod once per TCP connection, and gRPC reuses one connection for thousands of calls.
The decision has to be made per HTTP/2 stream, which needs something that understands HTTP/2.

incidents.title: Health checks pass on a dying node
incidents.brief: ShopFast's 10-node checkout fleet serves 18,000 req/s. 4% of checkouts hang for 5 s and time out, yet every node passes its health check.
incidents.constraint: The /healthz endpoint belongs to another team and can't be changed today.
incidents.question: How does the balancer stop sending checkouts to node 7?

choices.label: Passive outlier ejection on real timeouts and 5xx

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Catches gray failures from live traffic; needs an ejection cap.

choices.resultTitle: Node 7 ejected by its own responses
choices.resultBody: Envoy counts real failures: after 5 consecutive timeouts node 7 is ejected for 30 s, and re-ejected each time it returns, so checkout failures drop to 0.1%. Cost: cap ejections at 20% of the fleet so a bad deploy can't eject everything.

choices.label: Run the active health check every second instead of 10
choices.resultBody: The probe now runs ten times as often, but /healthz never touches the failing disk and keeps returning 200. Node 7 stays in rotation and 4% of checkouts still hang for 5 s.

nodes.sub: healthz 200 every 1 s, still in pool

choices.label: Retry timed-out checkout requests on another node
choices.resultBody: Retries mask most failed checkouts, so errors fall to 1.5% and p95 eases to 1.3 s. Node 7's NVMe error count doubled overnight.

hints: Node 7 reports healthy every time it is asked.
The health endpoint doesn't touch the disk that is failing.
The balancer already sees every real response and how long it took.

users: checkout timed out after 5.0 s (4% of attempts)
retry from the app succeeded on another attempt

culprit.explanation: Node 7's own log shows NVMe I/O timeouts and 4.8 s fsyncs on checkout writes, while /healthz, which never touches the disk, still answers 200 in 2 ms.

wrongNodeFeedback.lb: Envoy is doing what it was told: /healthz says every node is fine.
wrongNodeFeedback.ok: These nine nodes answer in 180 ms with fast disks.
wrongNodeFeedback.users: Shoppers only see the timeouts; the cause is behind the balancer.

incidents.title: Node 7 now fails 90% of checkouts
incidents.brief: Retries hid node 7 for a day. Its NVMe degraded overnight: 90% of its checkouts time out, each retry waits 5 s first, and 212 retried POSTs double-charged.
incidents.constraint: /healthz still can't be changed, and checkout POSTs are not idempotent.
incidents.question: What finally stops checkouts reaching node 7?

choices.label: Eject nodes after 5 consecutive real failures, not on healthz
choices.resultBody: Envoy's outlier detection ejects node 7 after five real timeouts and keeps re-ejecting it, so retries stop being needed; errors fall to 0.1% and the double charges stop. Replace the disk next.

choices.label: Raise the checkout retry count from 1 to 3 attempts per request
choices.resultBody: A doomed checkout now waits 5 s up to three times, p95 passes 10 s, and every extra retry of a non-idempotent POST risks another double charge.

choices.label: Cut the checkout timeout from 5 s to 1 s before retrying
choices.resultBody: The payment gateway's p99 is 1.5 s, so slow but healthy checkouts on good nodes are now cut and retried as well, and double charges triple.

hints: Node 7 still answers /healthz perfectly.
Retries treat the symptom and double-charge on the way.
The balancer already sees every real timeout node 7 produces.

incidents.title: Canary pods take half of production traffic
incidents.brief: StreamBox shipped playback API v2.3 as a canary meant to get 5% of 30,000 req/s. Both target groups are weighted 100, so the canary's 2 pods get 15,000 req/s and hit 97% CPU.
incidents.constraint: v2.3 must keep taking some live traffic so the release can still be evaluated.
incidents.question: How do you give the canary the slice it was meant to have?

choices.label: Weighted target groups at 95/5 with a stepped ramp

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Small blast radius; slower signal on rare bugs.

choices.resultBody: The listener now splits 95/5 per request: the canary's 2 pods get 1,500 req/s at about 45% CPU and v2.2 absorbs the rest at 60%. A ramp of 5, 25 and 50% with rollback on error rate follows. Cost: rare v2.3 bugs take longer to surface at 5%.

choices.label: Scale the canary to 20 pods to absorb its half
choices.resultTitle: Half of all viewers now on the canary
choices.resultBody: CPU recovers, but 50% of viewers now run unproven v2.3, and its codec regression fails 4% of its streams. Global playback errors settle at 2%, which is no longer a canary but a half-rollout.

choices.label: Set both groups to least-outstanding-requests
choices.resultBody: Least-outstanding-requests picks a pod inside each target group; it does not change the 100/100 weights between groups. The 2 canary pods still receive 15,000 req/s and stay at 96% CPU.

hints: Count the pods behind each target group.
Weights split traffic between groups, not between pods.
The canary's share is set on the listener rule and should grow in steps.

incidents.title: Least-connections floods a fast-failing node
incidents.brief: PayLink's 6 API nodes use least-connections at 15,000 req/s. Node 4 lost its database credentials and returns 500 in 3 ms, so it always has the fewest open connections and now gets 45% of requests.
incidents.constraint: Node 4 answers its TCP port check, so the balancer considers it healthy.
incidents.question: What keeps a node that fails fast from attracting traffic?

choices.label: Readiness probe that runs a real database query

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Probe detects broken dependencies; a shared-DB outage would fail every node at once.

choices.resultTitle: Broken node fails its readiness probe
choices.resultBody: HAProxy now calls /ready every 2 s, which runs SELECT 1 with the node's own credentials. Node 4 fails 3 probes and leaves the pool within 6 s; the other 5 nodes rise to 58% CPU and 5xx falls to 0.05%. Cost: keep the probe cheap and dependency-light.

choices.label: Switch HAProxy from leastconn to plain round-robin
choices.resultTitle: Black hole shrinks to one sixth
choices.resultBody: Round-robin stops rewarding node 4 for failing fast, so its share drops from 45% to about 17%. That is still one merchant payment in six returning 500, because the node remains in the pool.

choices.label: Add two more API nodes to dilute the bad one
choices.resultTitle: New nodes lose the race to node 4
choices.resultBody: The two new nodes hold real, slower connections, while node 4 still frees its connections in 3 ms. Leastconn keeps picking it, and 5xx only dips to 40%.

hints: A node that errors instantly always looks idle to least-connections.
An open TCP port says nothing about whether the node can reach its database.
The check that decides pool membership should exercise the dependency that broke.

incidents.title: DB failover empties the whole pool
incidents.brief: Readiness now runs a real query. During a 20 s database failover, all 6 nodes failed readiness together and HAProxy removed every one: 100% of payments got 503 for 26 s.
incidents.constraint: Readiness must still catch a single node with broken credentials, like node 4.
incidents.question: How do readiness checks survive a shared dependency blip?

choices.label: Fail open: keep all nodes in the pool when every probe fails
choices.resultBody: HAProxy ejects failing nodes only while most of the pool is healthy; when all six fail at once it keeps them, so a failover costs 20 s of slow queries, not a full outage. A lone broken node is still ejected.

choices.label: Restart HAProxy whenever the pool drops to zero nodes
choices.resultBody: The restarted HAProxy runs the same probes against the same failing database, so the pool is empty again within 6 s and the restart adds dropped connections on top.

choices.label: Take the database query back out of the readiness probe
choices.resultBody: The pool survives the next failover, but a node with broken credentials passes readiness again and least-connections floods it, which is last week's 45% error incident.

nodes.sub: broken node back in the pool

hints: Did six nodes break, or one thing they all share?
Ejecting every node never helps anyone.
When the whole pool fails at once, the pool is not the problem.

incidents.title: Orders service hammers one inventory pod
incidents.brief: The orders service resolves inventory.internal once at startup and caches the first IP forever. All 9,000 req/s land on 1 of 6 inventory pods at 98% CPU; the other five sit near 5%.
incidents.constraint: Inventory pods are replaced several times a day by the autoscaler.
incidents.question: How should orders spread its calls across inventory pods?

choices.label: Client-side balancing over live discovery endpoints

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Per-call balancing that follows pod churn; adds a discovery dependency.

choices.resultTitle: Calls spread over all live pods
choices.resultBody: A sidecar watches the endpoint list and balances each call with least-request, adding and dropping pods as the autoscaler replaces them. All six pods settle near 30% CPU and timeouts reach 0. Cost: every client now depends on the discovery system being healthy.

choices.label: Lower the DNS TTL on inventory.internal to 5 s
choices.resultBody: The DNS server now hands out a fresh answer every 5 s, but the orders JVM caches lookups forever and never asks again. Pod 1 still takes all 9,000 req/s at 98% CPU.

choices.label: Vertically scale the hot inventory pod to 8 vCPUs
choices.resultBody: CPU falls to 55% at first, but the resize reschedules the pod onto a new IP that orders never looks up. Orders keeps connecting to the old address, and a third of order calls now fail with connection refused.

hints: The other five pods are healthy and idle.
The client resolved a name once and never looked again.
Something on the calling side needs to track the current set of pods and pick one per request.

incidents.title: Every deploy wave cuts 2% of uploads
incidents.brief: CloudDocs deploys by removing a node from HAProxy and killing it 5 s later. Clients hold keep-alive connections for 60 s and uploads run up to 40 s, so each wave fails about 2% of 11,000 req/s.
incidents.constraint: The team deploys 15 times a day and won't stop shipping.
incidents.question: How do you take a node out without cutting live requests?

choices.label: Drain connections for 90 s before shutting down

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Clean deploys in exchange for slower rollouts.

choices.resultBody: HAProxy stops sending new requests to the draining node, which answers with Connection: close and finishes in-flight uploads. The process exits once its connections hit zero or 90 s pass, so deploy failures fall to 0.02%. Cost: each wave takes 90 s longer.

choices.label: Lower the keep-alive timeout to 5 seconds everywhere
choices.resultTitle: Handshakes up, long uploads still cut
choices.resultBody: Idle connections close sooner, but every reconnect now pays a TLS handshake and balancer CPU climbs to 70%. Uploads running 20-40 s are still in flight when the node is killed, so 1.2% of uploads keep failing.

choices.label: Batch all deploys into the 3 a.m. traffic trough
choices.resultBody: At 3 a.m. traffic is a quarter of peak, so fewer uploads are killed, but APAC users working at that hour still lose 2% of theirs. Fifteen changes now ship in one risky batch each night.

hints: The node is removed from the pool, yet it is still working when it dies.
Existing keep-alive connections and long uploads outlive a 5-second grace period.
Shutdown should wait on what the node is still doing, not on a fixed timer.

incidents.title: TLS errors on one in four new connections
incidents.brief: FinTrack's layer-4 NLB passes TLS straight through to 12 nodes that each hold their own certificate. Rotation failed on 3 nodes and their certificates expired at midnight; TCP health checks still pass.
incidents.constraint: Certificates rotate every 60 days, and the rotation script has failed twice this year.
incidents.question: What removes per-node certificates as a failure point?

choices.label: Terminate TLS at the balancer with one managed cert

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Central certificate and HTTP visibility; balancer sees decrypted traffic.

choices.resultTitle: One auto-renewed certificate at the edge
choices.resultBody: An L7 balancer now holds a single auto-renewed certificate and re-encrypts to the nodes with an internal CA, so handshake failures drop to 0. It can also see HTTP status codes for health and routing. Cost: about 15% more balancer CPU for handshakes.

choices.label: Switch the health checks from TCP to HTTP on port 80
choices.resultBody: Plain HTTP on port 80 never performs a TLS handshake, so the 3 nodes with expired certificates answer 200 and stay in the pool. One new connection in four still fails.

choices.label: Pull the three bad nodes and run on the other nine
choices.resultTitle: Nine nodes can't carry twelve's load
choices.resultBody: Handshake errors stop, but 26,000 req/s now land on 9 nodes and CPU climbs from 72% to 96%. p95 reaches 1.1 s, 3% of requests time out, and the next failed rotation repeats the incident.

hints: A TCP check only proves the port accepts connections.
Twelve copies of a certificate means twelve chances for rotation to fail.
A balancer that speaks HTTP could own the certificate itself.

incidents.title: Node crash empties 12% of carts mid on-sale
incidents.brief: TicketHub pins each shopper to 1 of 8 nodes with a cookie, and carts live in node memory. Node 3 crashed during a 20,000 req/s on-sale, logging out 12% of shoppers and emptying their carts.
incidents.constraint: Nodes will crash again; the fix must survive the next one without losing carts.
incidents.question: What lets any node serve a shopper after their node dies?

choices.label: Store carts in Redis so any node can serve any user

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Stateless nodes; Redis becomes a dependency to replicate.

choices.resultBody: Carts and sessions move to a replicated Redis cluster, and affinity is turned off. When a node dies, its shoppers land on another node with their carts intact, and load evens out at 70% CPU. Cost: about 0.5 ms per request for the Redis round trip.

choices.label: Rehash users with consistent hashing on node loss
choices.resultTitle: Fewer users moved, carts still lost
choices.resultBody: Consistent hashing moves only node 3's shoppers instead of reshuffling everyone, but their carts were in node 3's memory. The 12% still arrive at a node that has never seen them.

choices.label: Replicate every session to all eight nodes
choices.resultBody: Carts now survive a crash, but each cart update is copied to 7 peers and every node holds all sessions. During the on-sale, replication pushes CPU to 94% and p95 to 1.6 s.

hints: The balancer did route shoppers away from node 3.
Changing which node a shopper lands on doesn't bring their data along.
If no node owns the cart, losing a node can't lose it.

incidents.title: One Redis shard pegged at 100%
incidents.brief: Carts moved to a 6-shard Redis cluster. Every page view also reads the event's seat-map key, so its shard takes 60,000 reads/s at 100% CPU while five shards idle.
incidents.constraint: The seat map changes every few seconds; carts must stay in Redis.
incidents.question: How do you take the hot key off its shard?

choices.label: Cache the seat map in each node's memory for one second
choices.resultBody: Each of the 8 nodes reads the seat map from Redis once a second instead of 7,500 times, so shard 3 falls to 20% CPU. Seats can look up to 1 s stale, and checkout re-validates them.

choices.label: Add two more shards so the cluster spreads its keyspace wider
choices.resultBody: A single key hashes to one slot on one shard however many shards exist; the resharding adds load of its own and shard 3 stays at 100%.

choices.label: Raise the Redis client timeout from 200 ms to 2 s
choices.resultBody: Fewer calls time out, but requests queue behind the saturated shard, p95 climbs to 2 s, and page views pile up on the app nodes.

hints: How many shards can one key live on?
Every page asks for the same few bytes.
Serve a read-mostly key from closer than Redis.

incidents.title: Retry storm buries the surviving search nodes
incidents.brief: One of 5 search nodes died and clients retried each failed call 3 times with no delay. Load on the 4 survivors jumped from 20,000 to 52,000 req/s, and they started timing out too.
incidents.constraint: The dead node needs 15 minutes to be replaced.
incidents.question: How do you stop retries from multiplying the load?

choices.label: Retry budget of 10% with jittered back-off

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Bounded amplification; some failures surface to users.

choices.resultTitle: Retries shrink back to a trickle
choices.resultBody: Envoy allows retries only while they stay under 10% of active requests, spaced with jittered exponential backoff. Load falls to about 22,000 req/s, the 4 nodes settle at 80% CPU, and errors drop to 1%. Cost: during a real outage some calls fail instead of being retried.

choices.label: Raise the per-call timeout from 1 s to 10 s
choices.resultTitle: Slow calls now hog every connection
choices.resultBody: Fewer calls time out, but each stuck call now holds a connection 10 times longer. Connection pools on the 4 nodes fill up, queued searches wait, and p95 climbs to 9 s while retries continue.

choices.label: Autoscale search nodes when CPU passes 70%
choices.resultBody: New nodes take 4 minutes to boot and another 3 to load the index. By then the retry storm has pushed the survivors into restart loops, and each new node is flooded with 13,000 req/s the moment it joins.

hints: Real demand is still 20,000 req/s; the rest is retries.
Every failed call can turn into four calls on already struggling nodes.
Retries need a limit tied to overall traffic, and spacing so they don't arrive together.

knob.label: Retry budget
knob.question: Set the retry budget so failed calls get a second try without multiplying load.

low.title: No second chances
low.body: Under a 5% budget almost nothing is retried, so every transient timeout on the four busy survivors reaches a user and errors sit near 4%.

high.title: Retries swamp the survivors
high.body: Above 20%, retries become real load: a 50% budget turns 20,000 req/s of demand into 30,000 and pushes the four nodes to 95% CPU; 300% is the 52,000 req/s storm.

good.title: Retries back to a trickle
good.body: Real demand is 20,000 req/s; a 5-20% budget adds at most 4,000 retries, so four nodes carry about 22,000 req/s near 80% CPU and transient failures still get a second try.

incidents.title: Anycast routes players into a dead PoP
incidents.brief: GameNet announces one anycast /24 from 14 PoPs. Frankfurt's proxies crashed on a bad config, but its routers still announce the prefix, so 18% of 350,000 player sessions hit a PoP that drops them.
incidents.constraint: The BGP routers announce routes on their own and don't know whether the proxies are alive.
incidents.question: How should a PoP stop attracting traffic it can't serve?

choices.label: Tie each PoP's BGP announcement to proxy health

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Self-healing edge; needs dampening against flaps.

choices.resultBody: A health daemon next to the routers withdraws the anycast prefix when local proxies fail their checks. BGP reconverges in about 60 s and Frankfurt's players shift to Amsterdam and Paris, which rise to 68% CPU. Cost: add hold-down timers so a flapping PoP doesn't churn routes.

choices.label: Repoint the game hostname to Amsterdam's unicast IP
choices.resultBody: Resolvers and game clients cache the old anycast address for hours, so only 30% of affected players move. Everyone who does move now sends traffic to a single Amsterdam address, bypassing the other 12 PoPs.

choices.label: Prepend the AS path three times from Frankfurt
choices.resultBody: Distant networks now prefer other PoPs, but local peers at the Frankfurt exchange set a higher local-preference for peering routes, which beats AS-path length. They keep sending players into the dead PoP, and 11% of sessions still drop.

hints: Anycast sends packets to whichever PoP BGP says is closest.
Frankfurt still looks like a valid route because the announcement never stopped.
The route announcement should depend on whether the PoP can actually serve.

incidents.title: Every node slows down together
incidents.brief: OrderHub's 6 API nodes all run v4.2, which leaks about 1 GB of heap a day. Heap is at 88% on every node, and GC pauses push p99 to 2.4 s at 12,000 req/s.
incidents.constraint: The leak fix ships in tomorrow's release, and a fresh process takes about three days to leak back to this level.
incidents.question: What gets p99 back tonight?

choices.label: Drain and restart each leaking node, one at a time

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: A 20-minute rolling restart buys three days of headroom; it treats the symptom until the real fix ships.

choices.resultTitle: Fresh heaps, p99 back to normal
choices.resultBody: The balancer drains one node at a time, so five nodes always carry traffic while the sixth restarts. Each fresh process starts near 30% heap, GC pauses vanish, and p99 falls to 120 ms. The leak is still there, but it cannot bite again before tomorrow's fix.

choices.label: Enable outlier ejection so slow nodes leave the pool
choices.resultBody: All six nodes leak at the same rate, so none looks worse than its peers. Ejection compares nodes against each other, finds no outlier, and every node stays in the pool with 88% heap.

choices.label: Cut balancer timeouts and retry slow calls on another node
choices.resultTitle: Retries land on equally sick nodes
choices.resultBody: Every node pauses for GC, so a retried call usually hits another pause. Retries add about 25% more load, allocation speeds up, heap reaches 91%, and p99 gets worse.

hints: Compare the nodes with each other. Is any one of them worse?
The fix is already written; you only need to survive until it ships.
What resets a leaked heap without dropping live requests?
